title: telegram-notify.yml interpolates workflow_run context directly into a run: shell step
body:
## Description

The `release` job in the Telegram-notify workflow inlines `workflow_run` event context directly into the body of a `run:` shell step using `${{ ... }}` interpolation, instead of passing it through an `env:` variable:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/telegram-notify.yml:56-60
      - name: Extract version from tag
        id: ver
        run: |
          TAG=$(git describe --tags --exact-match "${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_sha }}" 2>/dev/null || echo "")
          if [ -z "$TAG" ]; then
```

With `${{ ... }}` interpolation, GitHub Actions performs **string substitution into the script text before the shell parses it**. This is the canonical script-injection anti-pattern (CWE-94 / GitHub "untrusted input in run step"): any `workflow_run` field placed here is concatenated into the command line rather than bound to a quoted variable. The same workflow already demonstrates the safe pattern a few lines above — the `commit` job passes the genuinely free-form `head_commit.message` through `env: FULL:` and references it as `"$FULL"` (lines 17-23) — but the `release` job interpolates `head_sha` straight into the `git describe` command.

Note: `github.event.workflow_run.head_sha` is a 40-character commit SHA, so practical injection through *this specific* field is constrained by GitHub's SHA format. The defect is the **pattern**: `workflow_run` is a privileged trigger that runs in the context of the default branch with read/write `GITHUB_TOKEN` access (see the missing-`permissions` finding), and interpolating any of its fields into `run:` is flagged by static analyzers (zizmor, CodeQL) precisely because the trust boundary is easy to widen by accident — a later edit that adds `head_commit.message` or `head_branch` to this block would become directly exploitable.

## Impact

Direct interpolation of `workflow_run` context into a shell step removes the env-var quoting boundary that prevents command injection. In a `workflow_run` trigger the job runs with elevated permissions and access to repository secrets (`TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN`, `TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID`), so a successful injection here would run attacker-chosen shell commands in a privileged CI context and could exfiltrate those secrets. The current `head_sha` value limits exploitability today, but the construct is a latent high-severity foot-gun and an inconsistency with the safe pattern used elsewhere in the same file.

## Required Fix

1. Move every `workflow_run`/event value out of the `run:` body into `env:` and reference it as a double-quoted shell variable, e.g. `env: HEAD_SHA: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_sha }}` then `git describe --tags --exact-match "$HEAD_SHA"`.
2. Audit all `run:` steps in the workflows for `${{ github.event.* }}` / `${{ github.head_ref }}` interpolation and convert them to the `env:`-variable form.
3. Add a CI lint (e.g. `zizmor` or `actionlint` with the relevant rule) to fail the build on direct interpolation of event context into `run:` steps.

## References

- GitHub: Security hardening for GitHub Actions — Understanding the risk of script injections — https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-guides/security-hardening-for-github-actions#understanding-the-risk-of-script-injections
- CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection') — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/94.html
- OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks — CICD-SEC-4: Poisoned Pipeline Execution — https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-ci-cd-security-risks/CICD-SEC-04-Poisoned-Pipeline-Execution

title: telegram-action third-party action pinned to mutable @master ref instead of a SHA
body:
## Description

The Telegram-notify workflow consumes the third-party action `appleboy/telegram-action` pinned to the branch ref `@master` in both jobs:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/telegram-notify.yml:36-43
      - name: Send commit to Telegram
        uses: appleboy/telegram-action@master
        with:
          to: ${{ secrets.TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID }}
          token: ${{ secrets.TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN }}
          format: html
          disable_web_page_preview: true
          message_file: .tg_message.txt
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/telegram-notify.yml:71
        uses: appleboy/telegram-action@master
```

`@master` is a **mutable branch pointer**: whatever commit `master` points to at run time is fetched and executed. The maintainer (or anyone who compromises that account/branch) can change the code behind this ref at any moment with no change to this repository. This action is invoked in a `workflow_run` context with the `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` and `TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID` secrets passed in via `with:`, so it already has access to repository secrets.

## Impact

Pinning to a mutable branch means the project has no control over, and no record of, the exact code it runs. A malicious or compromised update to `appleboy/telegram-action@master` would execute in CI with the Telegram bot token and chat id available, enabling secret exfiltration or arbitrary actions in the bot's chats — without any commit to this repo to review or roll back. This is a classic third-party-action supply-chain exposure (CICD-SEC-3 / dependency-confusion-adjacent), elevated by the secrets in scope.

## Required Fix

1. Pin the action to a full-length commit SHA (e.g. `appleboy/telegram-action@<40-char-sha>`) and add a trailing comment with the human-readable version, per GitHub's hardening guidance.
2. Verify the pinned SHA corresponds to a reviewed, released version, and adopt a process (or Dependabot, see the related finding) to bump the SHA deliberately.
3. Apply the same SHA-pinning to all third-party (non-`actions/*`) actions across the workflows.

## References

- GitHub: Security hardening for GitHub Actions — Using third-party actions / pin to a full-length commit SHA — https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-guides/security-hardening-for-github-actions#using-third-party-actions
- OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks — CICD-SEC-3: Dependency Chain Abuse — https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-ci-cd-security-risks/CICD-SEC-03-Dependency-Chain-Abuse
- CWE-829: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/829.html

title: CI, deploy-vercel, and telegram-notify workflows declare no permissions: (broad default GITHUB_TOKEN)
body:
## Description

Three of the four workflows declare no `permissions:` block at any level, so each job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` is granted the repository/organization **default** scopes. Only `release.yml` sets explicit permissions:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml:1-13 — no permissions: key anywhere
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  lint:
```

`deploy-vercel.yml` (lines 1-14) and `telegram-notify.yml` (lines 1-16) likewise have no `permissions:` declaration, while `release.yml:7-9` correctly scopes `contents: write` / `packages: write`. When `permissions:` is omitted, the token inherits the default token scopes, which on many repositories is the legacy broad/`read-write` set spanning `contents`, `issues`, `pull-requests`, `packages`, and more. `telegram-notify.yml` is especially sensitive because it runs on the privileged `workflow_run` trigger.

## Impact

Workflows run with more `GITHUB_TOKEN` authority than they need (none of these three jobs write to the repo via the token; CI only builds/tests, deploy uses a separate `VERCEL_TOKEN`, and notify only reads). An injected step or a compromised third-party action (see the `@master` and tag-pinning findings) would inherit those excess scopes and could push commits, open/close issues and PRs, or publish packages. Least-privilege tokens are a core CI/CD hardening control; the inconsistency (one workflow scoped, three unscoped) shows the omission is accidental. Severity **high** given the `workflow_run` trigger and the secrets handled in these files.

## Required Fix

1. Add a top-level `permissions: contents: read` to `ci.yml`, `deploy-vercel.yml`, and `telegram-notify.yml`, then grant any additional scope only on the specific job that needs it.
2. Set the repository/organization default `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions to read-only so unscoped workflows fail closed.
3. Re-confirm `release.yml` grants only the scopes it uses (`contents: write` for the GitHub release, `packages: write` for GHCR).

## References

- GitHub: Assigning permissions to jobs / restricting GITHUB_TOKEN permissions — https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-guides/automatic-token-authentication#modifying-the-permissions-for-the-github_token
- OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks — CICD-SEC-5: Insufficient PBAC (Pipeline-Based Access Controls) — https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-ci-cd-security-risks/CICD-SEC-05-Insufficient-PBAC
- CWE-250: Execution with Unnecessary Privileges — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/250.html

title: Core runtime dependency telegram resolves to a GitHub fork of gramjs, not the published package
body:
## Description

The `telegram` (gramjs) library — the MTProto client at the heart of the agent's Telegram connectivity — is declared not as the published npm package but as a Git dependency pointing at a third-party GitHub fork:

```json
// package.json:97
    "telegram": "github:TONresistor/gramjs#34b6b63",
```

The lockfile resolves this to `git+ssh://git@github.com/TONresistor/gramjs.git#34b6b63e513caa66fa26a98f81e43a70567a4953` (`package-lock.json:15190`). The ref *is* pinned to a commit SHA (`#34b6b63...`), which prevents silent content drift for that exact commit, so this is **not** a mutable-ref problem like `@master`. The supply-chain concern is the **source and trust model**: the project's primary Telegram transport is sourced from a personal fork (`TONresistor/gramjs`) rather than the upstream `telegram` npm release line. That means it bypasses npm's published-package provenance, receives no upstream security patches automatically, is not covered by `npm audit`/`audit-ci` advisory matching the same way a registry package is, and depends on the continued availability and integrity of that GitHub account and repository.

## Impact

A fork-by-SHA dependency for a network-facing, credential-handling core library concentrates supply-chain risk on a single third-party account: if the fork is deleted, made private, or its account is compromised and history is rewritten, installs break or (in the rewrite case, were the ref ever moved) could pull altered code. It also diverges from upstream gramjs security fixes, so CVEs patched upstream will not flow in without a manual re-fork/re-pin. Severity **high** because this is the Telegram session/auth transport (handling MTProto auth keys and message traffic), but mitigated relative to a branch ref because the commit SHA is pinned.

## Required Fix

1. Prefer the upstream published package (`telegram`/gramjs from npm) at a pinned version if the fork's changes are not strictly required.
2. If the fork is required, document **why** (which patches), vendor or mirror it under an organization-controlled namespace, and add the integrity hash verification (the lockfile pins the SHA — ensure CI installs from the lockfile only).
3. Track upstream gramjs advisories and establish a process to rebase the fork onto upstream security releases.

## References

- OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks — CICD-SEC-3: Dependency Chain Abuse — https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-ci-cd-security-risks/CICD-SEC-03-Dependency-Chain-Abuse
- CWE-1357: Reliance on Insufficiently Trustworthy Component — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1357.html
- npm docs: GitHub URLs as dependencies (semantics of `github:user/repo#commit-ish`) — https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/configuring-npm/package-json#github-urls

title: Dockerfile runs dependency lifecycle scripts during npm ci (no --ignore-scripts)
body:
## Description

Both the build stage and the runtime stage of the root `Dockerfile` run `npm ci` **without** `--ignore-scripts`, so every dependency's `preinstall`/`install`/`postinstall` lifecycle script executes during image build:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile:20-21 (build stage)
# Install all deps (including devDependencies for build + all workspaces)
RUN npm ci
```

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile:46-50 (runtime stage)
# Copy package files and install production deps only
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm pkg delete scripts.prepare \
    && npm ci --omit=dev \
    && npm cache clean --force
```

Line 48 only deletes the project's **own** `prepare` script; it does nothing to suppress lifecycle scripts belonging to the (transitive) dependency tree. This is notably inconsistent with the CI workflows, which deliberately install with the hardened flag everywhere — e.g. `.github/workflows/ci.yml:23` `npm ci --ignore-scripts` (and again at lines 36, 51, 70, 87, 103) and `release.yml:22`. The Docker image therefore executes arbitrary install-time code from dependencies that CI explicitly refuses to run.

## Impact

Malicious or compromised install scripts in any direct or transitive dependency run with full privileges of the Docker build (network + filesystem access) and are baked into the published `ghcr.io/...:latest` / version image that `release.yml` pushes and that `install.sh` pulls. Given this project also pulls a core dependency from a GitHub fork (see related finding), unguarded lifecycle execution materially widens the supply-chain attack surface at the exact point where artifacts are published to users. The mismatch with CI's `--ignore-scripts` policy means the protection the team already adopted is silently bypassed in the shipping image.

## Required Fix

1. Add `--ignore-scripts` to both `npm ci` invocations (Dockerfile:21 and Dockerfile:49), matching the CI policy.
2. Because native modules (`better-sqlite3`, `sqlite-vec`) need compilation, run an explicit, scoped rebuild after install (e.g. `npm rebuild better-sqlite3 sqlite-vec`, as `ci.yml:52` already does) rather than relying on arbitrary postinstall hooks.
3. Consider `npm ci --ignore-scripts --omit=dev` plus the scoped rebuild in the runtime stage so production installs never execute third-party scripts.

## References

- OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks — CICD-SEC-3: Dependency Chain Abuse — https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-ci-cd-security-risks/CICD-SEC-03-Dependency-Chain-Abuse
- CWE-829: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/829.html
- npm docs: `--ignore-scripts` and lifecycle scripts — https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/using-npm/scripts#best-practices

title: install.sh is delivered via curl | bash with no checksum or signature verification
body:
## Description

The documented installation method pipes a remotely-fetched script straight into a shell, and the script itself then fetches and executes further code with no integrity verification at any step:

```bash
# install.sh:5-6 (documented usage)
# Usage: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xlabtg/teleton-agent-v2/main/install.sh | bash
```

```bash
# install.sh:60  (npm path)
  if npm install -g "${NPM_PACKAGE}"; then
# install.sh:75  (docker path)
  if docker pull "${DOCKER_IMAGE}"; then
# install.sh:101 (git path)
    git clone "https://github.com/${REPO}.git" "${install_dir}"
```

The `curl ... | bash` entrypoint fetches `install.sh` from a mutable branch (`main`) over the network and executes it immediately, with no pinned commit, no published SHA-256 to compare, and no GPG/cosign signature check. The artifacts it subsequently installs (`npm install -g`, `docker pull ...:latest`, `git clone ... && npm install && npm run build`) are likewise taken on trust — the Docker image is the mutable `:latest` tag (line 10), and the npm/git paths run install-time scripts.

## Impact

Anyone able to tamper with the fetched bytes — a compromised CDN/MITM on the unauthenticated fetch, or a push to `main` — can achieve arbitrary code execution on the installing user's machine, since the output is executed verbatim by `bash`. There is no out-of-band way for a user to verify they ran the intended script. This is the well-known `curl | bash` trust problem; it is **medium** because it requires either transport compromise or repo compromise, but the blast radius (RCE on every installer) is high.

## Required Fix

1. Publish a SHA-256 checksum (and ideally a GPG or cosign signature) for `install.sh` and document a verify-then-run flow (`curl -o install.sh ... && sha256sum -c ... && bash install.sh`).
2. Pin the installer and the artifacts it fetches to immutable identifiers — a tagged release of `install.sh`, a versioned npm spec, and a digest-pinned Docker image instead of `:latest`.
3. Verify downloaded artifacts inside the script (e.g. compare the Docker image digest, use `npm ci` against a pinned version, or verify a release signature) before installing/building.

## References

- OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks — CICD-SEC-3: Dependency Chain Abuse — https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-ci-cd-security-risks/CICD-SEC-03-Dependency-Chain-Abuse
- CWE-494: Download of Code Without Integrity Check — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/494.html
- CWE-829: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/829.html

title: install.sh suggests sudo npm install -g, running a network install as root
body:
## Description

When the unprivileged global npm install fails, `install.sh` instructs the user to re-run it as root:

```bash
# install.sh:57-69
install_npm() {
  info "Installing via npm..."
  if npm install -g "${NPM_PACKAGE}"; then
    ok "Teleton installed via npm"
    # ...next steps...
  else
    error "npm install failed. Try: sudo npm install -g ${NPM_PACKAGE}"
  fi
}
```

`sudo npm install -g <pkg>` runs the entire dependency install — including any dependency lifecycle scripts (`preinstall`/`postinstall`) — as **root**. Because nothing else in this project guards global installs with `--ignore-scripts` (and the Docker image likewise runs lifecycle scripts, see the related finding), this guidance hands root-level execution to arbitrary package code as the project's documented remediation for a permissions error.

## Impact

Following this advice grants any malicious or compromised (transitive) dependency root on the user's system at install time, and produces root-owned files in the global `node_modules`/prefix that can cause later permission problems. The usual cause of the original EACCES failure is a root-owned npm prefix; recommending `sudo` treats the symptom while escalating privilege. Severity **medium**: it requires the user to follow the suggestion and a malicious dependency to be present, but the consequence is full root compromise.

## Required Fix

1. Replace the `sudo` suggestion with guidance to fix npm prefix ownership or use a user-writable prefix (e.g. set `npm config set prefix "$HOME/.npm-global"` and add it to `PATH`), or use a version manager (nvm/fnm) so global installs never need root.
2. If a privileged install is genuinely required, document running it with `--ignore-scripts` and a scoped rebuild instead of unrestricted root install.
3. Detect the EACCES/permission case and print the prefix-relocation remedy rather than `sudo`.

## References

- npm docs: Resolving EACCES permissions errors when installing packages globally (recommends a user-owned prefix, not sudo) — https://docs.npmjs.com/resolving-eacces-permissions-errors-when-installing-packages-globally
- CWE-250: Execution with Unnecessary Privileges — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/250.html
- CWE-426: Untrusted Search Path / privileged install hazards — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/426.html

title: Release workflow publishes a mutable :latest Docker tag with no immutable digest reference
body:
## Description

The release workflow builds and pushes the container image to GHCR under both a version tag and the floating `:latest` tag:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/release.yml:32-38
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: |
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.ref_name }}
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
```

The `:latest` tag is mutable — each release re-points it at a new image — and nothing in the pipeline records or surfaces the resulting image **digest** (`sha256:...`). Downstream, `install.sh:10` consumes exactly this mutable tag (`DOCKER_IMAGE="ghcr.io/${REPO}:latest"`) and `docker pull`s it (line 75), so users always run "whatever `:latest` is now" with no way to pin or verify which build they received.

## Impact

Mutable tags make deployments non-reproducible and undermine auditability and rollback: two `docker pull ...:latest` at different times can yield different code with no version signal, and there is no immutable handle for incident response or supply-chain attestation. If the registry or the publishing token is compromised, `:latest` can be silently overwritten and every consumer that pulls it is affected. Severity **medium**: it weakens integrity/reproducibility of the release channel rather than being directly exploitable on its own.

## Required Fix

1. Continue publishing the immutable version tag (`:${{ github.ref_name }}`) and treat it as the canonical reference; document pulling by version or by digest rather than `:latest`.
2. Capture and surface the pushed image digest (the `docker/build-push-action` `outputs.digest`) in the release notes / job summary so consumers can pin `ghcr.io/...@sha256:<digest>`.
3. Point `install.sh` and docs at a pinned version/digest by default, and consider enabling registry image immutability/attestation (e.g. provenance/SBOM, cosign signing).

## References

- OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks — CICD-SEC-1: Insufficient Flow Control Mechanisms / artifact integrity — https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-ci-cd-security-risks/
- CWE-494: Download of Code Without Integrity Check — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/494.html
- Docker: Pull an image by digest (immutable identifier) — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/image/pull/#pull-an-image-by-digest-immutable-identifier

title: First-party GitHub Actions are pinned to mutable major tags rather than commit SHAs
body:
## Description

Every action reference across the workflows is pinned to a **mutable tag** (`@v2`/`@v3`/`@v4`/`@v5`) rather than a full-length commit SHA. Examples:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml:18-19
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
# ci.yml:54 actions/upload-artifact@v4
# release.yml:27 docker/login-action@v3
# release.yml:32 docker/build-push-action@v5
# release.yml:41 softprops/action-gh-release@v2
# deploy-vercel.yml:15-16 actions/checkout@v4 / actions/setup-node@v4
```

A tag such as `@v4` is a moving pointer that the action's maintainer can repoint to any commit at any time. (`appleboy/telegram-action@master` is tracked separately as a higher-severity case because a branch ref is even more volatile and runs with secrets.) GitHub's hardening guidance is to pin third-party — and ideally all — actions to an immutable commit SHA so the executed code cannot change underneath the repository.

## Impact

If any referenced action's tag is repointed to malicious code (via a compromised maintainer account or a tag-move), it executes in this project's CI on the next run with whatever `GITHUB_TOKEN` scope and secrets that job carries — and several of these workflows lack a least-privilege `permissions:` block (see related finding), widening the blast radius. Tag-based pinning provides no record of the exact code that ran. Severity **medium**: `actions/*` and the listed vendors are reputable and `vN` tags are conventionally stable, but the repointing risk is real and the mitigation is cheap.

## Required Fix

1. Pin actions to full-length commit SHAs with a trailing version comment, e.g. `uses: actions/checkout@<40-char-sha> # v4.x`.
2. Adopt Dependabot for the `github-actions` ecosystem (see the missing-Dependabot finding) so SHA pins are bumped automatically with reviewable PRs.
3. Optionally enforce SHA pinning in CI via `actionlint`/`zizmor` and an allowlist of trusted actions.

## References

- GitHub: Security hardening for GitHub Actions — Using third-party actions (pin to a full-length commit SHA) — https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-guides/security-hardening-for-github-actions#using-third-party-actions
- OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks — CICD-SEC-3: Dependency Chain Abuse — https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-ci-cd-security-risks/CICD-SEC-03-Dependency-Chain-Abuse
- CWE-829: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/829.html

title: Repository has no Dependabot configuration and no CODEOWNERS file
body:
## Description

The `.github/` directory contains `workflows/`, `ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`, and `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`, but no automated-dependency-update configuration and no code-ownership file:

- No `.github/dependabot.yml` (and no Renovate config such as `renovate.json`) — confirmed absent by directory listing.
- No `.github/CODEOWNERS` (nor at repo root or `docs/`) — confirmed absent.

The project pins all GitHub Actions to mutable tags (see related finding), pulls a core dependency from a GitHub fork, and maintains a substantial npm dependency tree plus a sizeable `audit-ci.jsonc` advisory allowlist — all of which require ongoing, deliberate update and review. Without Dependabot/Renovate there is no automation surfacing new dependency or action versions and security patches; without CODEOWNERS there is no enforced reviewer for security-sensitive paths (workflows, `Dockerfile`, `install.sh`, `package.json`).

## Impact

Dependencies and pinned actions drift out of date and miss security fixes unless someone updates them by hand, increasing exposure to known vulnerabilities (the large advisory allowlist makes this worse). The absence of CODEOWNERS means changes to CI/CD, packaging, and supply-chain-critical files are not guaranteed to be reviewed by a designated owner — relevant given the script-injection and token-permission findings in these same files. Severity **medium**: this is a missing preventative/process control rather than an active vulnerability.

## Required Fix

1. Add `.github/dependabot.yml` covering the `npm` and `github-actions` ecosystems (and the `docker` ecosystem for the Dockerfiles) with a sensible schedule and grouping.
2. Add a `.github/CODEOWNERS` assigning required reviewers to security-sensitive paths: `.github/workflows/`, `Dockerfile`, `docker/`, `install.sh`, `package.json`, `audit-ci.jsonc`.
3. Enable branch-protection rules that require CODEOWNERS review for those paths.

## References

- GitHub: Configuring Dependabot version updates — https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/dependabot/dependabot-version-updates/configuring-dependabot-version-updates
- GitHub: About code owners (CODEOWNERS) — https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-code-owners
- OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks — CICD-SEC-3: Dependency Chain Abuse — https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-ci-cd-security-risks/CICD-SEC-03-Dependency-Chain-Abuse

title: audit-ci.jsonc allowlists 16 advisories, suppressing known vulnerabilities in CI
body:
## Description

The security-audit gate (`npm run security:audit` -> `audit-ci --moderate --config audit-ci.jsonc`, see `package.json:55`) allowlists sixteen advisory IDs, so any vulnerability matching one of these GHSA identifiers is ignored and the CI `Security Audit` job (`ci.yml:94-104`) passes regardless:

```jsonc
// audit-ci.jsonc:1-20
{
  "critical": true,
  "allowlist": [
    "GHSA-27v5-c462-wpq7",
    "GHSA-3v7f-55p6-f55p",
    "GHSA-48c2-rrv3-qjmp",
    "GHSA-4w7w-66w2-5vf9",
    "GHSA-67mh-4wv8-2f99",
    // ... 11 more GHSA ids ...
    "GHSA-xpcf-pg52-r92g"
  ]
}
```

Each entry permanently suppresses that advisory with no inline justification, no scope (the IDs are not tied to a specific package/path), and no expiry. There is no comment recording why each was accepted or when it should be revisited, and the related missing-Dependabot finding means nothing is driving the underlying dependencies forward so these can be removed.

## Impact

Allowlisting is a blanket mute: a suppressed advisory will not fail CI even if a future dependency change makes it reachable/exploitable, and undocumented entries tend to become permanent, growing the project's accepted-risk debt invisibly. With 16 muted advisories the audit gate provides materially weaker assurance than it appears to. Severity **medium**: suppressing advisories is sometimes legitimate (false positives, unreachable code), but doing so unscoped, unjustified, and unexpiring is a supply-chain hygiene weakness.

## Required Fix

1. For each allowlisted GHSA, add an inline justification comment (why it is not exploitable here, the affected package, and a review/expiry date), or remove it.
2. Prefer remediation over suppression: upgrade or override the vulnerable transitive dependency (the repo already uses `overrides` in `package.json`) so the advisory no longer applies.
3. Periodically re-audit the allowlist (ideally driven by Dependabot updates) and delete entries that no longer match the resolved tree.

## References

- OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks — CICD-SEC-3: Dependency Chain Abuse — https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-ci-cd-security-risks/CICD-SEC-03-Dependency-Chain-Abuse
- CWE-1104: Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1104.html
- audit-ci docs: allowlist semantics — https://github.com/IBM/audit-ci#options

title: docker/rvc image runs as root, uses a floating base tag, and has no HEALTHCHECK
body:
## Description

The `docker/rvc` voice-conversion image is built without container-hardening basics:

```dockerfile
# docker/rvc/Dockerfile:4-34 (excerpt)
FROM python:3.10-slim

WORKDIR /app
# ... apt-get install ffmpeg/gcc/g++ ... pip install torch ... ...
COPY inference.py /app/inference.py
RUN mkdir -p /app/models /app/input /app/output

ENTRYPOINT ["python", "/app/inference.py"]
```

Three issues:
1. **Runs as root** — there is no `USER` directive, so the container's default user is `root`; the entrypoint and all file I/O under `/app/{models,input,output}` run as uid 0.
2. **Floating base tag** — `FROM python:3.10-slim` pins only the minor line (3.10), not a patch version or an immutable digest, so rebuilds silently pull a different base image. (Note: this is a *floating* tag, not the `:latest` tag as originally suspected — the severity of the base-image issue is correspondingly lower.)
3. **No `HEALTHCHECK`** — unlike the main `Dockerfile` (which defines one at line 72), this image declares none, so orchestrators cannot detect a hung/unhealthy inference process.

## Impact

Running as root means any code-execution or path-traversal bug in the inference path (which processes external audio/model inputs) executes with full in-container root, and mounted volumes get root-owned files. The floating base tag makes builds non-reproducible and may pull in unvetted base changes. The missing healthcheck reduces operability. Severity **low**: this is an auxiliary, opt-in image (not the primary published agent image) and the base tag is pinned to a minor version rather than fully floating `:latest`, so the practical exposure is limited.

## Required Fix

1. Add a non-root user (e.g. `RUN useradd -m app && chown -R app /app` then `USER app`) and ensure `/app/{input,output,models}` are writable by that user.
2. Pin the base image to a specific patch tag and ideally a digest (`FROM python:3.10.<x>-slim@sha256:<digest>`).
3. Add a `HEALTHCHECK` appropriate to the inference process (or document that it is a short-lived batch container if a healthcheck is not meaningful).

## References

- Docker: Best practices — run as a non-root user / `USER` — https://docs.docker.com/build/building/best-practices/#user
- CWE-250: Execution with Unnecessary Privileges — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/250.html
- CWE-1104: Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components (floating base image) — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1104.html

title: Main Dockerfile leaves build toolchain in the final image (bloat / attack surface)
rejectionReason: The runtime stage explicitly removes the build toolchain. After installing production deps (Dockerfile:48-50, which need python3/make/g++ to compile native modules such as better-sqlite3), Dockerfile:53 runs `RUN apt-get purge -y python3 make g++ && apt-get autoremove -y`, so python3/make/g++ are not present in the final image's top filesystem layer. The build toolchain that IS installed only for compilation lives in the separate `build` stage (Dockerfile:7-11), which is discarded and never copied into the runtime stage (only `dist/` and `configs/` are copied via `COPY --from=build`). The finding's premise — that the final image retains the build toolchain — does not hold against the current code. (Minor, non-defect note: because the purge at line 53 is a separate RUN layer from the install at line 48-50, the toolchain still occupies intermediate layer history and so does not shrink the image as much as installing+purging in a single RUN would; this is a marginal size optimization, not the security/bloat defect described, and removing the runtime toolchain entirely would break the native-module rebuild, so the minimal-fix constraint precludes simply deleting it.)
body:
## Description

This suspected finding claims the main `Dockerfile` leaves the build toolchain (`python3`, `make`, `g++`) in the final published image. On inspection of the current runtime stage, the toolchain is installed only to compile native modules during `npm ci --omit=dev` and is then explicitly purged:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile:39-53 (runtime stage)
# Runtime deps for native modules
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
    python3 \
    make \
    g++ \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm pkg delete scripts.prepare \
    && npm ci --omit=dev \
    && npm cache clean --force

# Remove build tools (no longer needed after native compilation)
RUN apt-get purge -y python3 make g++ && apt-get autoremove -y
```

The finding does not reproduce: the final image does not retain the toolchain.

## Impact

Not applicable — rejected.

## Required Fix

None. See `rejectionReason` for the marginal (non-defect) layer-squashing observation.

## References

- Docker: Best practices — minimize the number of layers / multi-stage builds — https://docs.docker.com/build/building/best-practices/

title: PR template instructs targeting a nonexistent dev branch; SECURITY.md points to the wrong repo URL
body:
## Description

Two project documents contain contradictory/incorrect references to this repository.

1. The pull-request template tells contributors to target a `dev` branch that does not exist:

```markdown
<!-- .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md:15-16 -->
- [ ] I have read the [Contributing Guide](../CONTRIBUTING.md)
- [ ] My PR targets the `dev` branch (not `main`)
```

This directly contradicts `CONTRIBUTING.md:66`, which states: "All work happens on **`main`**. There is no `dev` branch." The repository confirms there is no `dev` branch (only `main` and per-issue branches).

2. `SECURITY.md` directs vulnerability reports to the wrong repository's advisory page:

```markdown
<!-- SECURITY.md:18 -->
- **GitHub Security Advisories**: [Report a vulnerability](https://github.com/TONresistor/teleton-agent/security/advisories/new)
```

The actual repository is `github.com/xlabtg/teleton-agent-v2` (per `package.json` name `teleton-agent-v2` and the git remote), not `TONresistor/teleton-agent`, so the advisory link points to the wrong (or nonexistent) project.

## Impact

Contributors who follow the PR template will set the wrong base branch and have their PRs bounced or mis-targeted, adding friction and confusion. More importantly, the wrong `SECURITY.md` advisory URL can route security reporters to a different/incorrect repository — or a dead link — defeating the purpose of a responsible-disclosure policy and risking that a real vulnerability report never reaches the maintainers. Severity **low** (documentation), but the security-reporting misdirection is the more consequential half.

## Required Fix

1. Update `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md:16` to reference `main` (e.g. "My PR targets the `main` branch"), consistent with `CONTRIBUTING.md`.
2. Correct the `SECURITY.md` advisory link to the canonical repository (`https://github.com/xlabtg/teleton-agent-v2/security/advisories/new`) and re-check the other contact details.
3. Grep the docs for any other stale `TONresistor/teleton-agent` or `dev`-branch references and fix them.

## References

- GitHub: Privately reporting a security vulnerability / security advisories — https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/security-advisories/working-with-repository-security-advisories/about-repository-security-advisories

title: .dockerignore does not exclude *.pem / *.key, risking secret leakage into build context
body:
## Description

The `.dockerignore` excludes several secret-bearing files but omits private-key and certificate material:

```gitignore
# .dockerignore (full)
node_modules
dist
.git
.github
.husky
.reference
.vscode
.idea
.obsidian

*.log
*.db
*.session
*.session-journal
.env
.DS_Store

config.yaml
wallet.json
telegram_session.txt
telegram-offset.json
```

There are no `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.crt`, `*.p12`, or `id_rsa`-style entries. This project generates and uses TLS material at runtime — it depends on `selfsigned` (`package.json:95`) for self-signed certificates and the WebUI supports HTTPS — so `.pem`/`.key` files can plausibly exist in the working tree. Anything not excluded here is sent to the Docker daemon as build context and can be inadvertently `COPY`'d into an image (the Dockerfile uses broad directory copies such as `COPY configs/ configs/`).

## Impact

If a developer or CI checkout has a private key or certificate in the build context (e.g. a generated `*.pem`/`*.key`, or an SSH key), it can be copied into the image and published to GHCR via the release workflow, leaking the private key to anyone who pulls the image. Even without an explicit `COPY`, the key bytes are transmitted to the build daemon. Severity **low**: it depends on such a file being present in the context, but the consequence (private-key disclosure in a published image) is serious, and the fix is trivial and purely additive.

## Required Fix

1. Add private-key/certificate patterns to `.dockerignore`: `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.crt`, `*.cer`, `*.p12`, `*.pfx`, and `id_rsa*`.
2. Prefer explicit allow-listing in the Dockerfile (copy only the specific files/dirs needed) over broad `COPY dir/ dir/` to reduce accidental inclusion.
3. Add a CI check that fails if key/cert material appears in the build context.

## References

- Docker: Build context and `.dockerignore` file — https://docs.docker.com/build/concepts/context/#dockerignore-files
- CWE-312: Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/312.html
- CWE-538: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Externally-Accessible File or Directory — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/538.html
